# fancy_regex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fancy-regex/0.18.0/fancy_regex/index.html

## Expand description

An implementation of regexes, supporting a relatively rich set of features, including backreferences and lookaround. Aims to be compatible with Oniguruma syntax when the relevant flag is set.

It builds on top of the excellent [regex](https://crates.io/crates/regex) crate. If you are not
familiar with it, make sure you read its documentation and maybe you don’t even need fancy-regex.

If your regex or parts of it does not use any special features, the matching is delegated to the regex crate. That means it has linear runtime. But if you use “fancy” features such as backreferences or look-around, an engine with backtracking needs to be used. In that case, the regex can be slow and take exponential time to run because of what is called “catastrophic backtracking”. This depends on the regex and the input.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The API should feel very similar to the regex crate, and involves compiling a regex and then using it to find matches in text.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-matching-text)Example: Matching text

An example with backreferences to check if a text consists of two identical words:

```
use fancy_regex::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"^(\w+) (\1)$").unwrap();
let result = re.is_match("foo foo");
assert!(result.is_ok());
let did_match = result.unwrap();
assert!(did_match);
```
Note that like in the regex crate, the regex needs anchors like `^` and `$` to match against the
entire input text.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-finding-the-position-of-matches)Example: Finding the position of matches

```
use fancy_regex::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"(\d)\1").unwrap();
let result = re.find("foo 22");
assert!(result.is_ok(), "execution was successful");
let match_option = result.unwrap();
assert!(match_option.is_some(), "found a match");
let m = match_option.unwrap();
assert_eq!(m.start(), 4);
assert_eq!(m.end(), 6);
assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "22");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-capturing-groups)Example: Capturing groups

```
use fancy_regex::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"(?<!AU)\$(\d+)").unwrap();
let result = re.captures("AU$10, $20");
let captures = result.expect("Error running regex").expect("No match found");
let group = captures.get(1).expect("No group");
assert_eq!(group.as_str(), "20");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-splitting-text)Example: Splitting text

```
use fancy_regex::Regex;
let re = Regex::new(r"[ \t]+").unwrap();
let target = "a b \t  c\td    e";
let fields: Vec<&str> = re.split(target).map(|x| x.unwrap()).collect();
assert_eq!(fields, vec!["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]);
let fields: Vec<&str> = re.splitn(target, 3).map(|x| x.unwrap()).collect();
assert_eq!(fields, vec!["a", "b", "c\td    e"]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

This crate supports several optional features that can be enabled or disabled:

- `std`- `no_std`environments.
- `unicode`
- `perf`
- `variable-lookbehinds`- `(?<=a+)`). Without this feature, only constant-length lookbehinds are supported. This feature uses reverse DFA matching from the- `regex-automata`crate to efficiently handle variable-length patterns that don’t use backreferences or other fancy features.

[§](https://docs.rs#syntax)Syntax

The regex syntax is based on the [regex](https://crates.io/crates/regex) crate’s and on Oniguruma, with some additional supported syntax.
Where the two conflict, there is a flag to prefer Oniguruma parsing rules. (By default `regex` crate compatible parsing is used.)

Escapes:

`\h`
: hex digit (`[0-9A-Fa-f]`)

`\H`
: not hex digit (`[^0-9A-Fa-f]`)

`\e`
: escape control character (`\x1B`)

`\K`
: keep text matched so far out of the overall match ([docs](https://www.regular-expressions.info/keep.html))

`\G`
: anchor to where the previous match ended ([docs](https://www.regular-expressions.info/continue.html))

`\Z`
: anchor to the end of the text before any trailing newlines

`\O`
: any character including newline

`\N`
: any character except newline

`\R`
: general newline - matches all common line break characters: \n, \v, \f, \r, treating \r\n as an atomic unit

Backreferences:

`\1`
: match the exact string that the first capture group matched

`\2`
: backref to the second capture group, etc.

`\k<name>`
: match the exact string that the capture group named *name* matched

`(?P=name)`
: same as `\k<name>` for compatibility with Python, etc.

`\g<name>`
: call the subroutine defined in capture group named *name*

`\g<1>`
: call the subroutine defined in capture group 1. Subroutines can be recursive up to 20 levels deep.

Named capture groups:

`(?<name>exp)`
: match *exp*, creating capture group named *name*

`(?P<name>exp)`
: same as `(?<name>exp)` for compatibility with Python, etc.

Look-around assertions for matching without changing the current position:

`(?=exp)`
: look-ahead, succeeds if *exp* matches to the right of the current position

`(?!exp)`
: negative look-ahead, succeeds if *exp* doesn’t match to the right

`(?<=exp)`
: look-behind, succeeds if *exp* matches to the left of the current position

`(?<!exp)`
: negative look-behind, succeeds if *exp* doesn’t match to the left

**Note**: Look-behind assertions with variable length (e.g., `(?<=a+)`) are supported with the
`variable-lookbehinds` feature (enabled by default). Without this feature, only constant-length
look-behinds are supported. Variable-length look-behinds can include word boundaries and other
zero-width assertions (e.g., `(?<=\ba+)`) as long as the rest of the pattern doesn’t use
backreferences or other “fancy” features that require backtracking within the lookbehind.

Atomic groups using `(?>exp)` to prevent backtracking within `exp`, e.g.:

```
let re = Regex::new(r"^a(?>bc|b)c$").unwrap();
assert!(re.is_match("abcc").unwrap());
// Doesn't match because `|b` is never tried because of the atomic group
assert!(!re.is_match("abc").unwrap());
```
Conditionals - if/then/else:

`(?(1))`
: continue only if first capture group matched

`(?(<name>))` or `(?('name'))`
: continue only if capture group named *name* matched

`(?(1)true_branch|false_branch)`
: if the first capture group matched then execute the true_branch regex expression, else execute false_branch ([docs](https://www.regular-expressions.info/conditional.html))

`(?(condition)true_branch|false_branch)`
: if the condition matches then execute the true_branch regex expression, else execute false_branch from the point just before the condition was evaluated

`(?(DEFINE)(capture group)(?<named_group>another)`
: define capture groups for later use in subroutine calls

Backtracking control verbs:

`(*FAIL)`
: fail the current backtracking branch

Absent repeater:

`(?~abc)`
: match anything until `abc` would match or until the end of the haystack if no match

[§](https://docs.rs#subroutines-reusable-patterns-with-stable-meaning)Subroutines: reusable patterns with stable meaning

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-a-subroutine)What is a subroutine

Subroutines in fancy-regex are *compiled pattern definitions* that can be invoked safely and predictably.
Any capture group can become a subroutine - it just needs to be “called”.

`(?<num>\d*\.\d+|\d+) x \g<num>`In the above example, a capture group called `num` is defined, to match numbers with or without decimal places. `\g<num>` executes the capture group again, without the author having to re-type the pattern inside it.
The above pattern would match text like `5.2 x 6` for instance.

Think of a subroutine as:

- defined by a capture group
- executed exactly the way the capture group was originally defined
- reusable from multiple places

[§](https://docs.rs#side-effects)Side effects

A subroutine call has one side-effect - it updates the capture group position, which affects backref matching etc.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Let’s imagine a pattern which will match a digit and capture it into group 1. Then it will call that capture group as a subroutine. Then it will do a backref to group 1.

This will match three consecutive digits. The 2nd and 3rd digits must be identical.

```
use fancy_regex::{Error, Regex};
let re = Regex::new(r"(\d)\g<1>\1")?;
let result = re.captures("foo 711")?;
let captures = result.unwrap();
let m = captures.get(0).unwrap();
assert_eq!(m.start(), 4);
assert_eq!(m.end(), 7);
assert_eq!(m.as_str(), "711");
let group = captures.get(1).unwrap();
assert_eq!(group.as_str(), "1");
assert!(!re.is_match("foo 717")?);
```
In the above example, 7 was stored in capture group 1. Then it was replaced with 1 by the subroutine call. Then the backreference to group 1 can only match the literal `1`.

[§](https://docs.rs#side-effect-edge-cases)Side effect edge cases

Also, in a lookbehind, a subroutine call would not update the capture group position when the currently stored position for that capture group is further to the right in the haystack. i.e. right-most captures take precedence.

[§](https://docs.rs#flags-and-the-common-misconception)Flags and the common misconception

When subroutines are first introduced, a very common assumption is:

“If I apply flags at the call site, they should affect the subroutine.”

This assumption is reasonable — many regex engines either behave this way or do not specify the behavior clearly.
**fancy-regex does not do this**, and the reason is central to its design.

Let’s look at a concrete example.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-pattern)The pattern

`\A(?<word>[a-z]+)\s+(?i:\g<word>)`[§](https://docs.rs#the-input)The input

`hello Mr`At first glance, this pattern appears to say:

- At the beginning of the input string
- Match a word of lowercase letters and capture it as `word`
- Match some whitespace
- Call the subroutine `word`, but case-insensitively

Many users therefore expect this pattern to match the input above.

**It does not.**

[§](https://docs.rs#what-actually-happens)What actually happens

The key to understanding this behavior is that **flags belong to the subroutine definition, not the call site**.

Let’s walk through the execution step by step.

[§](https://docs.rs#execution-trace)Execution trace

[§](https://docs.rs#step-1-assert-position-at-the-beginning-of-the-input-string)Step 1: Assert position at the beginning of the input string

- Pattern: `\A`
- Active flags: none
- Input position: 0 (start of `"hello Mr"`)

[§](https://docs.rs#step-2-enter-subroutine-definition-word)Step 2: Enter subroutine definition `word`

- Pattern: `[a-z]+`
- Active flags: none
- Input position: 0 (start of `"hello Mr"`)

The engine greedily matches `[a-z]+` against `"hello"`.
The range 0 - 5 is stored in capture group 1, whose name is `word`.

[§](https://docs.rs#step-3-exit-subroutine-definition-word-and-continue-matching)Step 3: Exit subroutine definition `word` and continue matching

- Pattern: `\s+`
- Active flags: none
- Input position: 5 (at the space after `hello`)

The engine matches `\s+` against `" "`.

[§](https://docs.rs#step-4-call-subroutine-word)Step 4: Call subroutine `word`

- Pattern: `\g<word>`->`(?<word>[a-z]+)`
- Active flags: none - because the capture group definition had no flags active
- Input position: 6 (after `" "`at the`'M'`of`"Mr"`)

This fails immediately, because:

- The pattern is case-sensitive
- The first character is `'M'`, which does not fall in the range a-z.

[§](https://docs.rs#step-5-no-alternatives-available)Step 5: No alternatives available

- There are no alternations inside `word`
- There are no backtracking points before the failure
- The anchor prevents us from trying other starting positions in the input string

The match fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-the-i-flag-did-not-apply)Why the `i` flag did not apply

The `i` flag appears **only at the call site**:

`(?i:\g<word>)`However, calling a subroutine does **not** re-evaluate or modify its definition.

The subroutine `word` was compiled once, with these properties:

- Pattern: `[a-z]+`
- Flags: none
- Capture group number: 1

When the subroutine is called, the engine:

- Enters the already-compiled definition
- Executes it exactly as defined
- Ignores any flags applied at the call site

[§](https://docs.rs#this-is-a-feature-not-a-limitation)This is a feature, not a limitation

fancy-regex deliberately enforces this rule to guarantee that:

- A subroutine behaves the same everywhere it is used
- Flags cannot silently change the meaning of a reused pattern
- There is no “action at a distance” from call sites

If call-site flags were allowed to affect subroutines, the same subroutine could behave differently depending on where it was called - making patterns harder to reason about and easier to misuse.

[§](https://docs.rs#expressing-the-intended-behavior)Expressing the intended behavior

If the intent is for `word` to be matched case-insensitively, the flag must be applied **at the definition**:

`(?i:(?<word>[a-z]+))\s+\g<word>`or

`(?<word>(?i:[a-z]+))\s+\g<word>`Now the subroutine is compiled with the `i` flag, and every call to it behaves consistently.

[§](https://docs.rs#key-takeaway)Key takeaway

Subroutines in fancy-regex are compiled once, with fixed flags.Call sites cannot change their behavior.

This rule enables safe reuse, predictable execution, and clear reasoning - especially in larger and more complex patterns. It also matches Oniguruma behavior, so if you plan to use fancy-regex as a memory-safe alternative, you can!

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-rejection-of-left-recursive-patterns)Compile-time rejection of left-recursive patterns

fancy-regex’s support of subroutines unlocks powerful features such as recursion. With that power comes the risk of defining patterns that can recurse forever.

To guarantee termination and predictable behavior, fancy-regex rejects left-recursive patterns at compile time.

This check is conservative: if a pattern could recurse without consuming input, it is rejected - even if a particular input would not trigger that behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-left-recursion)What is left recursion?

A pattern is left-recursive if it can re-enter itself without consuming any input.

In other words, the engine can make recursive calls while staying at the same input position.

A simplified example looks like this:

`(?<expr>\g<expr>a|a)`Here, the subroutine expr can immediately call itself before matching anything. No matter what the input is, this definition allows infinite recursion.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-fancy-regex-rejects-these-patterns)Why fancy-regex rejects these patterns

Left recursion is problematic because:

- It can cause infinite recursion or unbounded backtracking
- It cannot be made safe by input inspection alone

Even if a specific input would not trigger the recursion, the pattern itself is unsafe.

Rather than attempting to detect or recover from such cases at runtime, fancy-regex enforces a stronger rule:

**Every recursive call must consume input before it can recurse again.**

This guarantees that evaluation always makes progress.

[§](https://docs.rs#conservative-by-design)Conservative by design

The left-recursion check is intentionally conservative.

Consider the following pattern:

`(?<expr>ab|\g<expr>a)`For the input “ab”, this pattern would terminate successfully. However, fancy-regex still rejects it.

Why?

Because the second alternative allows recursion before any input is consumed. The engine cannot rely on runtime input to guarantee termination.

This is a deliberate design choice:

fancy-regex validates the structure of the pattern, not the behavior of a particular input.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-allowed)What is allowed

Recursive patterns are allowed as long as they consume input before recursing.

For example:

`(?<paren>\((?:[^()]*|\g<paren>)\))`Here:

- Each recursive call to `paren`is preceded by a literal ‘(’
- Input is always consumed before recursion
- Termination is guaranteed

This kind of recursion is safe and fully supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-restructure-left-recursive-patterns)How to restructure left-recursive patterns

Left-recursive definitions can often be rewritten in a right-recursive or iterative form.

For example, instead of:

`(?<expr>\g<expr>a|a)`You can write:

`a+`Or, when recursion is genuinely required:

`(?<expr>a\g<expr>?)`In this version, input is consumed before the recursive call, satisfying fancy-regex’s safety rules.

[§](https://docs.rs#recursion)Recursion

Recursion is when a subroutine calls itself, directly or indirectly.

[§](https://docs.rs#depth-limit)Depth limit

fancy-regex supports recursion up to 20 levels deep.

Let’s look at a simple example to prove this:

`(a\g<1>?)`Here we have a pattern which defines capture group 1 as consuming the literal `a`, followed by calling itself between 0 and 1 times greedily.

With 22 `a` characters as input, only 20 are matched:

```
use fancy_regex::{Error, Regex};
let pattern = r"(a\g<1>?)";
let re = Regex::new(pattern)?;
let haystack = "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"; // 22 a's
let result = re.find(haystack)?;
let found = result.unwrap();
// match is limited to 20 characters due to recursion depth limit
assert_eq!(found.as_str().len(), 20);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#unbounded-recursion)Unbounded recursion

fancy-regex will return a compile error for patterns which recurse indefinitely.

Let’s look at a simple example to prove this:

`(a\g<1>)`Here, capture group 1 consumes the literal `a`, then calls itself unconditionally. After recursion level 20 is reached, there is not a single path which would return a match.

[§](https://docs.rs#side-effects-1)Side effects

You may remember that it was stated earlier that the side effect of a subroutine call is that the capture group will be updated. It would be more accurate to say that the capture group is updated for non-recursive subroutine calls only.

Why?

Imagine a pattern like:

`(?<foo>a|\(\g<foo>\))`It will match the literal `a`, or any number of balanced parenthesis surrounding `a`.
If the recursive subroutine call would update the capture group start position, the opening parenthesis would not be included in the capture group.
If the recursive subroutine call would update the capture group end position (as well), you’d get the inner most subroutine call’s start position and outer most subroutine call’s end position, which would then be overridden anyway when the capture group at the root level is exited.
This would produce exceptionally odd and confusing behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#backreferences)Backreferences

fancy-regex does not yet support relative recursion level backreferences, and attempting to backreference a capture group which is currently being recursed is at present a compile error.

Example (adapting the previous pattern):

`(?<foo>a|\(\g<foo>\)\k<foo>?)`With an input like:

`(((a)(a)))`Oniguruma would give you two matches - the two `(a)`s.
fancy-regex would give (if the compile error were removed and no other changes made,) a single match of `(a)(a`, which is clearly not what anyone would expect.
fancy-regex prefers correctness and rejects such patterns rather than exhibiting undefined behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#absent-operators)Absent Operators

The absent operators are worth talking about because they are quite uncommon.

[§](https://docs.rs#absent-repeater)Absent Repeater

An absent repeater node is defined by the syntax `(?~inner_pattern)`, and it will match any text where the inner pattern does not match (i.e. is absent), including across newlines.
This does not add any new abilities to the engine, it just allows to clarify intent and to be more easily optimized under the hood. fancy-regex mainly implements this for Oniguruma compatibility.

It works best or is at least easiest to understand when the inner pattern is a literal.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

Let’s imagine you have some Markdown, containing some code fences.

It might look something like this:

```
# Some Heading
Given a todo list like this:
**Input:**
```json
{
  "todos": [
    {
      "content": "Create `some_helper_func` helper in some_file.rs that takes a closure to check the error",
      "status": "complete",
      "priority": "high"
    },
    {
      "content": "Update error-asserting tests in some_file.rs to use `some_helper_func`",
      "status": "complete",
      "priority": "high"
    },
    {
      "content": "Run `cargo fmt` and `cargo test`",
      "status": "pending",
      "priority": "medium"
    }
  ]
}
```
You might expect this output:
**Output:**
```text
High priority tasks have now been completed.
```
Some more text.
```
Let’s say you want to match all input and output codeblocks.

Typically you *could* do it like:

`[*]{2}(?:In|Out)put:[*]{2}\n```(?:[^`]+|`(?!``))+````This would match everything inside the codeblock which is not a backtick, or backticks which are not followed by another 2 backticks, until it reaches the 3 backticks marking the end of the codeblock. Generally this type of construct can be quite hard to follow and reason about, to be sure it won’t suffer from catastrophic backtracking.

With the absent repeater, the intention becomes a lot easier to understand - match anything that isn’t 3 backticks, followed by 3 backticks.

`[*]{2}(?:In|Out)put:[*]{2}\n```(?~```)````Where it really shines is when you need more complicated expressions, like to match a variable number of backticks from the code fence boundaries, it becomes a lot easier to read than an expanded alternative which would avoid catastrophic backtracking.

```
use fancy_regex::Regex;
// Match a code fence: opening backticks (3+), content (absent the same backticks), closing backticks
let re = Regex::new(r"(?<!`)(`{3,}(?!`))\w*\n(?~\1)\n(\1)")?;
// A code fence with 4 backticks, where the inner code contains 3 backticks
let input = "````text\nsome code with ``` backticks\n````";
let captures = re.captures(input)?.expect("should match");
// The overall match spans the entire input
let m = captures.get(0).unwrap();
assert_eq!(m.start(), 0);
assert_eq!(m.end(), input.len());
assert_eq!(m.as_str(), input);
// Group 1: the opening 4 backticks
let open = captures.get(1).unwrap();
assert_eq!(open.as_str(), "````");
assert_eq!(open.start(), 0);
assert_eq!(open.end(), 4);
// Group 2: the closing 4 backticks
let close = captures.get(2).unwrap();
assert_eq!(close.as_str(), "````");
assert_eq!(close.start(), input.len() - 4);
assert_eq!(close.end(), input.len());
```
It also allows the engine to optimize it accordingly.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-ways-of-looking-at-it)Other ways of looking at it

The absent repeater can be considered shorthand for this:

`(?((?!absent))\O|)*`Essentially a conditional, which says when the absent expression doesn’t match, match a single character including newlines. When the absent expression does match, match nothing. Repeat greedily.

- [Capture](https://docs.rs/enum.CaptureGroupTarget.html)- Group - Target
- Target of a backreference or subroutine call
- [Compile](https://docs.rs/enum.CompileError.html)- Error
- An error as the result of compiling a regex.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An error as the result of parsing, compiling or running a regex.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.Expr.html)
- Regular expression AST. This is public for now but may change.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.ExprChildrenIter.html)- Children - Iter
- An iterator over the immediate children of an `Expr`
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/enum.ExprChildrenIterMut.html)- Children - Iter - Mut
- An iterator over the immediate children of an `Expr`
- [Look](https://docs.rs/enum.LookAround.html)- Around
- Type of look-around assertion as used for a look-around expression.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- An error for the result of parsing a regex pattern.
- [Runtime](https://docs.rs/enum.RuntimeError.html)- Error
- An error as the result of executing a regex.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Replacer](https://docs.rs/trait.Replacer.html)
- Replacer describes types that can be used to replace matches in a string.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [escape](https://docs.rs/fn.escape.html)
- Escapes special characters in `text`with ‘\’. Returns a string which, when interpreted as a regex, matches exactly`text`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Result type for this crate with specific error enum.

[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// An iterator over all non-overlapping matches for a particular string.
[129](https://docs.rs#129)///
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// The iterator yields a `Result<Match>`. The iterator stops when no more
[131](https://docs.rs#131)/// matches can be found.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)///
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// `'r` is the lifetime of the compiled regular expression and `'t` is the
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// lifetime of the matched string.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)#[derive(Debug)]
[136](https://docs.rs#136)pub struct Matches<'r, 't> {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    re: &'r Regex,
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    text: &'t str,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    last_end: usize,
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    last_match: Option<usize>,
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    last_skipped_empty: bool,
[142](https://docs.rs#142)}
[143](https://docs.rs#143)
[144](https://docs.rs#144)impl<'r, 't> Matches<'r, 't> {
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// Return the text being searched.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    pub fn text(&self) -> &'t str {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)        self.text
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    }
[149](https://docs.rs#149)
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    /// Return the underlying regex.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    pub fn regex(&self) -> &'r Regex {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)        self.re
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    /// Adapted from the `regex` crate. Calls `find_from_pos`/`captures_from_pos` repeatedly.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    /// Ignores empty matches immediately after a match.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    /// Also passes a flag when skipping an empty match, so that \G wouldn't match at the new start position.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)    fn next_with<F, R>(&mut self, mut search: F) -> Option<Result<R>>
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    where
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        F: FnMut(&Regex, usize, u32) -> Result<Option<(R, Match<'t>)>>,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)        if self.last_end > self.text.len() {
[163](https://docs.rs#163)            return None;
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)        let option_flags = if self.last_skipped_empty {
[167](https://docs.rs#167)            OPTION_SKIPPED_EMPTY_MATCH
[168](https://docs.rs#168)        } else {
[169](https://docs.rs#169)            0
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        };
[171](https://docs.rs#171)
[172](https://docs.rs#172)        let pos = self.last_end;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)        let (result, mat) = match search(self.re, pos, option_flags) {
[174](https://docs.rs#174)            Err(error) => {
[175](https://docs.rs#175)                // Stop on first error: If an error is encountered, return it, and set the "last match position"
[176](https://docs.rs#176)                // to the string length, so that the next next() call will return None, to prevent an infinite loop.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)                self.last_end = self.text.len() + 1;
[178](https://docs.rs#178)                return Some(Err(error));
[179](https://docs.rs#179)            }
[180](https://docs.rs#180)            Ok(None) => return None,
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            Ok(Some(pair)) => pair,
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        };
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)        if mat.start == mat.end {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)            // This is an empty match. To ensure we make progress, start
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            // the next search at the smallest possible starting position
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            // of the next match following this one.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)            self.last_end = next_utf8(self.text, mat.end);
[189](https://docs.rs#189)            // Only set OPTION_SKIPPED_EMPTY_MATCH on the next call if this was a
[190](https://docs.rs#190)            // truly zero-length match (the VM consumed no bytes from `pos`).
[191](https://docs.rs#191)            // This means that \K won't prevent \G from matching.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)            self.last_skipped_empty = mat.end == pos;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)            // Don't accept empty matches immediately following a match.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)            // Just move on to the next match.
[195](https://docs.rs#195)            if Some(mat.end) == self.last_match {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)                return self.next_with(search);
[197](https://docs.rs#197)            }
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        } else {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            self.last_end = mat.end;
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            self.last_skipped_empty = false;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)        }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)        self.last_match = Some(mat.end);
[204](https://docs.rs#204)
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        Some(Ok(result))
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    }
[207](https://docs.rs#207)}

[212](https://docs.rs#212)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {

[214](https://docs.rs#214)        self.next_with(move |re, pos, flags| {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)            re.find_from_pos_with_option_flags(text, pos, flags)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)                .map(|opt| opt.map(|m| (m, m)))
[217](https://docs.rs#217)        })
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    }

[290](https://docs.rs#290)/// An iterator over all substrings delimited by a regex.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)/// This iterator yields `Result<&'h str>`, where each item is a substring of the
[293](https://docs.rs#293)/// target string that is delimited by matches of the regular expression. It stops when there
[294](https://docs.rs#294)/// are no more substrings to yield.
[295](https://docs.rs#295)///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// `'r` is the lifetime of the compiled regular expression, and `'h` is the
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// lifetime of the target string being split.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)///
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// This iterator can be created by the [`Regex::split`] method.
[300](https://docs.rs#300)#[derive(Debug)]
[301](https://docs.rs#301)pub struct Split<'r, 'h> {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    matches: Matches<'r, 'h>,
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    next_start: usize,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    target: &'h str,
[305](https://docs.rs#305)}
[306](https://docs.rs#306)
[307](https://docs.rs#307)impl<'r, 'h> Iterator for Split<'r, 'h> {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    type Item = Result<&'h str>;
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// Returns the next substring that results from splitting the target string by the regex.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    ///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// If no more matches are found, returns the remaining part of the string,
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// or `None` if all substrings have been yielded.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Result<&'h str>> {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        match self.matches.next() {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)            None => {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)                let len = self.target.len();
[318](https://docs.rs#318)                if self.next_start > len {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)                    // No more substrings to return
[320](https://docs.rs#320)                    None
[321](https://docs.rs#321)                } else {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)                    // Return the last part of the target string
[323](https://docs.rs#323)                    // Next call will return None
[324](https://docs.rs#324)                    let part = &self.target[self.next_start..len];
[325](https://docs.rs#325)                    self.next_start = len + 1;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)                    Some(Ok(part))
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                }
[328](https://docs.rs#328)            }
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            // Return the next substring
[330](https://docs.rs#330)            Some(Ok(m)) => {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)                let part = &self.target[self.next_start..m.start()];
[332](https://docs.rs#332)                self.next_start = m.end();
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                Some(Ok(part))
[334](https://docs.rs#334)            }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            Some(Err(e)) => Some(Err(e)),
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        }
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)}
[339](https://docs.rs#339)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)impl<'r, 'h> core::iter::FusedIterator for Split<'r, 'h> {}
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)/// An iterator over at most `N` substrings delimited by a regex.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)///
[344](https://docs.rs#344)/// This iterator yields `Result<&'h str>`, where each item is a substring of the
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// target that is delimited by matches of the regular expression. It stops either when
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// there are no more substrings to yield, or after `N` substrings have been yielded.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// The `N`th substring is the remaining part of the target.
[349](https://docs.rs#349)///
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// `'r` is the lifetime of the compiled regular expression, and `'h` is the
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// lifetime of the target string being split.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)/// This iterator can be created by the [`Regex::splitn`] method.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)#[derive(Debug)]
[355](https://docs.rs#355)pub struct SplitN<'r, 'h> {
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    splits: Split<'r, 'h>,
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    limit: usize,
[358](https://docs.rs#358)}
[359](https://docs.rs#359)
[360](https://docs.rs#360)impl<'r, 'h> Iterator for SplitN<'r, 'h> {
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    type Item = Result<&'h str>;
[362](https://docs.rs#362)
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// Returns the next substring resulting from splitting the target by the regex,
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// limited to `N` splits.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    ///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// Returns `None` if no more matches are found or if the limit is reached after yielding
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// the remaining part of the target.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Result<&'h str>> {
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        if self.limit == 0 {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)            // Limit reached. No more substrings available.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)            return None;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        }
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        // Decrement the limit for each split.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        self.limit -= 1;
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        if self.limit > 0 {
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            return self.splits.next();
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        }
[379](https://docs.rs#379)
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        // Nth split
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        let len = self.splits.target.len();
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        if self.splits.next_start > len {
[383](https://docs.rs#383)            // No more substrings available.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)            None
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        } else {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            // Return the remaining part of the target
[387](https://docs.rs#387)            let start = self.splits.next_start;
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            self.splits.next_start = len + 1;
[389](https://docs.rs#389)            Some(Ok(&self.splits.target[start..len]))
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    }
[392](https://docs.rs#392)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        (0, Some(self.limit))
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    }
[396](https://docs.rs#396)}
[397](https://docs.rs#397)
[398](https://docs.rs#398)impl<'r, 'h> core::iter::FusedIterator for SplitN<'r, 'h> {}

[611](https://docs.rs#611)
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// Attempts to better match [Oniguruma](https://github.com/kkos/oniguruma)'s default behavior
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    ///
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// Currently this amounts to changing behavior with:
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    ///
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// # Left and right word bounds
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    ///
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// `fancy-regex` follows the default of other regex engines such as the `regex` crate itself
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// where `\<` and `\>` correspond to a _left_ and _right_ word-bound respectively. This
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    /// differs from Oniguruma's defaults which treat them as matching the literals `<` and `>`.
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    /// When this option is set using `\<` and `\>` in the pattern will match the literals
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    /// `<` and `>` instead of word bounds.
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    ///
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    /// # Repetition/Quantifiers on empty groups
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    ///
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// `fancy-regex` would normally reject patterns like `(?:)+` because the `+` has nothing
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    /// to target. In Oniguruma mode, the empty repeat is silently dropped at parse time.
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    ///
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    /// ## Example
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    ///
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    /// ```
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    /// use fancy_regex::{Regex, RegexBuilder};
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    ///
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    /// let haystack = "turbo::<Fish>";
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// let regex = r"\<\w*\>";
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    ///
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// // By default `\<` and `\>` will match the start and end of a word boundary
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    /// let word_bounds_regex = Regex::new(regex).unwrap();
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// let word_bounds = word_bounds_regex.find(haystack).unwrap().unwrap();
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// assert_eq!(word_bounds.as_str(), "turbo");
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    ///
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    /// // With the option set they instead match the literal `<` and `>` characters
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// let literals_regex = RegexBuilder::new(regex).oniguruma_mode(true).build().unwrap();
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    /// let literals = literals_regex.find(haystack).unwrap().unwrap();
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// assert_eq!(literals.as_str(), "<Fish>");
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    /// ```
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    pub fn oniguruma_mode(&mut self, yes: bool) -> &mut Self {
[648](https://docs.rs#648)        self.options.oniguruma_mode = yes;
[649](https://docs.rs#649)        self
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    }
[651](https://docs.rs#651)}
[652](https://docs.rs#652)

[668](https://docs.rs#668)

[779](https://docs.rs#779)impl Regex {
[780](https://docs.rs#780)    /// Parse and compile a regex with default options, see `RegexBuilder`.
[781](https://docs.rs#781)    ///
[782](https://docs.rs#782)    /// Returns an [`Error`](enum.Error.html) if the pattern could not be parsed.
[783](https://docs.rs#783)    pub fn new(re: &str) -> Result<Regex> {
[784](https://docs.rs#784)        Self::new_options(re.to_string(), &RegexOptions::default())
[785](https://docs.rs#785)    }
[786](https://docs.rs#786)
[787](https://docs.rs#787)    fn new_options(pattern: String, options: &RegexOptions) -> Result<Regex> {
[788](https://docs.rs#788)        let mut tree = Expr::parse_tree_with_flags(&pattern, options.compute_flags())?;
[789](https://docs.rs#789)
[790](https://docs.rs#790)        let find_not_empty = options.hard_regex_runtime_options.find_not_empty;
[791](https://docs.rs#791)
[792](https://docs.rs#792)        let requires_capture_group_fixup = if find_not_empty {
[793](https://docs.rs#793)            // if the find_not_empty flag is set, we skip optimizations
[794](https://docs.rs#794)            // partially because we have to go though the VM anyway
[795](https://docs.rs#795)            // partially because having the last instruction of the expression not have
[796](https://docs.rs#796)            // ix be at the end of capture group 0 ruins our empty match checking logic.
[797](https://docs.rs#797)            false
[798](https://docs.rs#798)        } else {
[799](https://docs.rs#799)            // try to optimize the expression tree so that a hard pattern could become easy
[800](https://docs.rs#800)            // with a fixup of the capture groups
[801](https://docs.rs#801)            optimize(&mut tree)
[802](https://docs.rs#802)        };
[803](https://docs.rs#803)        let info = analyze(
[804](https://docs.rs#804)            &tree,
[805](https://docs.rs#805)            AnalyzeContext {
[806](https://docs.rs#806)                explicit_capture_group_0: requires_capture_group_fixup,
[807](https://docs.rs#807)                find_not_empty,
[808](https://docs.rs#808)            },
[809](https://docs.rs#809)        )?;
[810](https://docs.rs#810)
[811](https://docs.rs#811)        if find_not_empty && info.const_size && info.min_size == 0 {
[812](https://docs.rs#812)            return Err(CompileError::PatternCanNeverMatch.into());
[813](https://docs.rs#813)        }
[814](https://docs.rs#814)
[815](https://docs.rs#815)        if !info.hard {
[816](https://docs.rs#816)            // easy case, wrap regex
[817](https://docs.rs#817)
[818](https://docs.rs#818)            // we do our own to_str because escapes are different
[819](https://docs.rs#819)            // NOTE: there is a good opportunity here to use Hir to avoid regex-automata re-parsing it
[820](https://docs.rs#820)            let mut re_cooked = String::new();
[821](https://docs.rs#821)            tree.expr.to_str(&mut re_cooked, 0);
[822](https://docs.rs#822)            let inner = compile::compile_inner(&re_cooked, options)?;
[823](https://docs.rs#823)            return Ok(Regex {
[824](https://docs.rs#824)                inner: RegexImpl::Wrap {
[825](https://docs.rs#825)                    inner,
[826](https://docs.rs#826)                    pattern,
[827](https://docs.rs#827)                    explicit_capture_group_0: requires_capture_group_fixup,
[828](https://docs.rs#828)                    delegated_pattern: re_cooked,
[829](https://docs.rs#829)                },
[830](https://docs.rs#830)                named_groups: Arc::new(tree.named_groups),
[831](https://docs.rs#831)            });
[832](https://docs.rs#832)        }
[833](https://docs.rs#833)
[834](https://docs.rs#834)        let prog = compile(
[835](https://docs.rs#835)            &info,
[836](https://docs.rs#836)            CompileOptions {
[837](https://docs.rs#837)                anchored: can_compile_as_anchored(&tree.expr),
[838](https://docs.rs#838)                contains_subroutines: tree.contains_subroutines,
[839](https://docs.rs#839)            },
[840](https://docs.rs#840)        )?;
[841](https://docs.rs#841)        Ok(Regex {
[842](https://docs.rs#842)            inner: RegexImpl::Fancy {
[843](https://docs.rs#843)                prog: Arc::new(prog),
[844](https://docs.rs#844)                n_groups: info.end_group(),
[845](https://docs.rs#845)                options: options.hard_regex_runtime_options,
[846](https://docs.rs#846)                pattern,
[847](https://docs.rs#847)            },
[848](https://docs.rs#848)            named_groups: Arc::new(tree.named_groups),
[849](https://docs.rs#849)        })
[850](https://docs.rs#850)    }
[851](https://docs.rs#851)
[852](https://docs.rs#852)    /// Returns the original string of this regex.
[853](https://docs.rs#853)    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str {
[854](https://docs.rs#854)        match &self.inner {
[855](https://docs.rs#855)            RegexImpl::Wrap { pattern, .. } => pattern,
[856](https://docs.rs#856)            RegexImpl::Fancy { pattern, .. } => pattern,
[857](https://docs.rs#857)        }
[858](https://docs.rs#858)    }

[875](https://docs.rs#875)            RegexImpl::Fancy { .. } => self.find(text).map(|m| m.is_some()),
[876](https://docs.rs#876)        }

[927](https://docs.rs#927)    /// Returns the first match in `text`, starting from the specified byte position `pos`.
[928](https://docs.rs#928)    ///
[929](https://docs.rs#929)    /// # Examples
[930](https://docs.rs#930)    ///
[931](https://docs.rs#931)    /// Finding match starting at a position:
[932](https://docs.rs#932)    ///
[933](https://docs.rs#933)    /// ```
[934](https://docs.rs#934)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[935](https://docs.rs#935)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(?m:^)(\d+)").unwrap();
[936](https://docs.rs#936)    /// let text = "1 test 123\n2 foo";
[937](https://docs.rs#937)    /// let mat = re.find_from_pos(text, 7).unwrap().unwrap();
[938](https://docs.rs#938)    ///
[939](https://docs.rs#939)    /// assert_eq!(mat.start(), 11);
[940](https://docs.rs#940)    /// assert_eq!(mat.end(), 12);
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    /// ```
[942](https://docs.rs#942)    ///
[943](https://docs.rs#943)    /// Note that in some cases this is not the same as using the `find`
[944](https://docs.rs#944)    /// method and passing a slice of the string, see [Regex::captures_from_pos()] for details.
[945](https://docs.rs#945)    pub fn find_from_pos<'t>(&self, text: &'t str, pos: usize) -> Result<Option<Match<'t>>> {
[946](https://docs.rs#946)        self.find_from_pos_with_option_flags(text, pos, 0)
[947](https://docs.rs#947)    }
[948](https://docs.rs#948)
[949](https://docs.rs#949)    fn find_from_pos_with_option_flags<'t>(
[950](https://docs.rs#950)        &self,
[951](https://docs.rs#951)        text: &'t str,
[952](https://docs.rs#952)        pos: usize,
[953](https://docs.rs#953)        option_flags: u32,
[954](https://docs.rs#954)    ) -> Result<Option<Match<'t>>> {
[955](https://docs.rs#955)        if pos > text.len() {
[956](https://docs.rs#956)            return Ok(None);
[957](https://docs.rs#957)        }
[958](https://docs.rs#958)        match &self.inner {
[959](https://docs.rs#959)            RegexImpl::Wrap {
[960](https://docs.rs#960)                inner,
[961](https://docs.rs#961)                explicit_capture_group_0,
[962](https://docs.rs#962)                ..
[963](https://docs.rs#963)            } => {
[964](https://docs.rs#964)                let result = if !*explicit_capture_group_0 {
[965](https://docs.rs#965)                    inner
[966](https://docs.rs#966)                        .search(&RaInput::new(text).span(pos..text.len()))
[967](https://docs.rs#967)                        .map(|m| Match::new(text, m.start(), m.end()))
[968](https://docs.rs#968)                } else {
[969](https://docs.rs#969)                    let mut locations = inner.create_captures();
[970](https://docs.rs#970)                    inner.captures(RaInput::new(text).span(pos..text.len()), &mut locations);
[971](https://docs.rs#971)                    locations
[972](https://docs.rs#972)                        .get_group(1)
[973](https://docs.rs#973)                        .map(|group1| Match::new(text, group1.start, group1.end))
[974](https://docs.rs#974)                };
[975](https://docs.rs#975)                Ok(result)
[976](https://docs.rs#976)            }
[977](https://docs.rs#977)            RegexImpl::Fancy { prog, options, .. } => {
[978](https://docs.rs#978)                let option_flags = option_flags
[979](https://docs.rs#979)                    | if options.find_not_empty {
[980](https://docs.rs#980)                        OPTION_FIND_NOT_EMPTY
[981](https://docs.rs#981)                    } else {
[982](https://docs.rs#982)                        0
[983](https://docs.rs#983)                    };
[984](https://docs.rs#984)                let result = vm::run(prog, text, pos, option_flags, options)?;
[985](https://docs.rs#985)                Ok(result.map(|saves| Match::new(text, saves[0], saves[1])))
[986](https://docs.rs#986)            }
[987](https://docs.rs#987)        }
[988](https://docs.rs#988)    }
[989](https://docs.rs#989)
[990](https://docs.rs#990)    /// Returns an iterator over all the non-overlapping capture groups matched in `text`.
[991](https://docs.rs#991)    ///
[992](https://docs.rs#992)    /// # Examples
[993](https://docs.rs#993)    ///

[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)    /// Returns the capture groups for the first match in `text`.
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)    ///
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)    /// If no match is found, then `Ok(None)` is returned.

[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)    ///
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)    /// Finding matches and capturing parts of the match:
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)    ///
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)    /// ```rust

[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})").unwrap();

[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)    /// ```
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)    pub fn captures<'t>(&self, text: &'t str) -> Result<Option<Captures<'t>>> {
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)        self.captures_from_pos(text, 0)

[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)    /// Returns the capture groups for the first match in `text`, starting from
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)    /// the specified byte position `pos`.
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)    ///
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)    /// # Examples
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)    ///
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)    /// Finding captures starting at a position:
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)    ///
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)    /// ```
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(?m:^)(\d+)").unwrap();
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)    /// let text = "1 test 123\n2 foo";
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)    /// let captures = re.captures_from_pos(text, 7).unwrap().unwrap();
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)    ///
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)    /// let group = captures.get(1).unwrap();
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)    /// assert_eq!(group.as_str(), "2");
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)    /// assert_eq!(group.start(), 11);
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)    /// assert_eq!(group.end(), 12);
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)    /// ```
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)    ///
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)    /// Note that in some cases this is not the same as using the `captures`
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)    /// method and passing a slice of the string, see the capture that we get
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)    /// when we do this:
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)    ///
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)    /// ```
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(?m:^)(\d+)").unwrap();
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)    /// let text = "1 test 123\n2 foo";
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)    /// let captures = re.captures(&text[7..]).unwrap().unwrap();
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)    /// assert_eq!(captures.get(1).unwrap().as_str(), "123");
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)    /// ```
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)    ///
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)    /// This matched the number "123" because it's at the beginning of the text
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)    /// of the string slice.
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)    ///
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)    pub fn captures_from_pos<'t>(&self, text: &'t str, pos: usize) -> Result<Option<Captures<'t>>> {
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)        self.captures_from_pos_with_option_flags(text, pos, 0)
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)    }
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)    fn captures_from_pos_with_option_flags<'t>(
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)        &self,
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)        text: &'t str,
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)        pos: usize,
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)        option_flags: u32,
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)    ) -> Result<Option<Captures<'t>>> {
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)        if pos > text.len() {
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)            return Ok(None);
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)        }
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)        let named_groups = self.named_groups.clone();
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)        match &self.inner {
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)            RegexImpl::Wrap {
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)                inner,
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)                explicit_capture_group_0,
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)                ..
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)            } => {
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)                // find_not_empty patterns are always compiled as Fancy, so find_not_empty is
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)                // always false here.
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)                let explicit = *explicit_capture_group_0;
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)                let mut locations = inner.create_captures();
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)                inner.captures(RaInput::new(text).span(pos..text.len()), &mut locations);
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)                Ok(locations.is_match().then_some(Captures {
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)                    inner: CapturesImpl::Wrap {
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)                        text,
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)                        locations,
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)                        explicit_capture_group_0: explicit,
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)                    },
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)                    named_groups,
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)                }))
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)            }
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)            RegexImpl::Fancy {

[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)                n_groups,
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)                options,
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)                ..
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)            } => {
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)                let option_flags = option_flags
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)                    | if options.find_not_empty {
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)                        OPTION_FIND_NOT_EMPTY
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)                    } else {
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)                        0
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)                    };
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)                let result = vm::run(prog, text, pos, option_flags, options)?;
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)                Ok(result.map(|mut saves| {
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)                    saves.truncate(n_groups * 2);
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)                    Captures {
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)                        inner: CapturesImpl::Fancy { text, saves },
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)                        named_groups,
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)                    }
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)                }))
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)            }
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)        }
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)    }

[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)    /// Returns the number of captures, including the implicit capture of the entire expression.
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)    pub fn captures_len(&self) -> usize {
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)        match &self.inner {
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)            RegexImpl::Wrap {
[1139](https://docs.rs#1139)                inner,
[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)                explicit_capture_group_0,
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)                ..
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)            } => inner.captures_len() - if *explicit_capture_group_0 { 1 } else { 0 },
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)            RegexImpl::Fancy { n_groups, .. } => *n_groups,
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)        }
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)    }

[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)        }
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)        CaptureNames(names.into_iter())
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)    }

[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)    /// Replaces the leftmost-first match with the replacement provided.
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)    /// The replacement can be a regular string (where `$N` and `$name` are
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)    /// expanded to match capture groups) or a function that takes the matches'
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)    /// `Captures` and returns the replaced string.
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)    ///
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)    /// If no match is found, then a copy of the string is returned unchanged.
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)    ///
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)    /// # Replacement string syntax
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)    ///
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)    /// All instances of `$name` in the replacement text is replaced with the
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)    /// corresponding capture group `name`.
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)    ///
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)    /// `name` may be an integer corresponding to the index of the
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)    /// capture group (counted by order of opening parenthesis where `0` is the
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)    /// entire match) or it can be a name (consisting of letters, digits or
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)    /// underscores) corresponding to a named capture group.
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)    ///
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)    /// If `name` isn't a valid capture group (whether the name doesn't exist
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)    /// or isn't a valid index), then it is replaced with the empty string.
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)    ///
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)    /// The longest possible name is used. e.g., `$1a` looks up the capture
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)    /// group named `1a` and not the capture group at index `1`. To exert more
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)    /// precise control over the name, use braces, e.g., `${1}a`.
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)    ///
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)    /// To write a literal `$` use `$$`.
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)    ///
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)    /// # Examples
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)    ///
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)    /// Note that this function is polymorphic with respect to the replacement.
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)    /// In typical usage, this can just be a normal string:
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)    ///
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)    /// ```rust
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)    /// let re = Regex::new("[^01]+").unwrap();
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)    /// assert_eq!(re.replace("1078910", ""), "1010");
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)    /// ```
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)    ///
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)    /// But anything satisfying the `Replacer` trait will work. For example,
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)    /// a closure of type `|&Captures| -> String` provides direct access to the
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)    /// captures corresponding to a match. This allows one to access
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)    /// capturing group matches easily:
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)    ///
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)    /// ```rust
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)    /// # use fancy_regex::{Regex, Captures};
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"([^,\s]+),\s+(\S+)").unwrap();
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)    /// let result = re.replace("Springsteen, Bruce", |caps: &Captures| {
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)    ///     format!("{} {}", &caps[2], &caps[1])
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)    /// });
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)    /// assert_eq!(result, "Bruce Springsteen");
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)    /// ```
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)    ///
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)    /// But this is a bit cumbersome to use all the time. Instead, a simple
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    /// syntax is supported that expands `$name` into the corresponding capture
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)    /// group. Here's the last example, but using this expansion technique
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)    /// with named capture groups:
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)    ///
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)    /// ```rust
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(?P<last>[^,\s]+),\s+(?P<first>\S+)").unwrap();
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)    /// let result = re.replace("Springsteen, Bruce", "$first $last");
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)    /// assert_eq!(result, "Bruce Springsteen");
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)    /// ```
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)    ///
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)    /// Note that using `$2` instead of `$first` or `$1` instead of `$last`
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)    /// would produce the same result. To write a literal `$` use `$$`.
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)    ///
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)    /// Sometimes the replacement string requires use of curly braces to
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)    /// delineate a capture group replacement and surrounding literal text.
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)    /// For example, if we wanted to join two words together with an
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    /// underscore:
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)    ///
[1247](https://docs.rs#1247)    /// ```rust
[1248](https://docs.rs#1248)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[1249](https://docs.rs#1249)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(?P<first>\w+)\s+(?P<second>\w+)").unwrap();
[1250](https://docs.rs#1250)    /// let result = re.replace("deep fried", "${first}_$second");
[1251](https://docs.rs#1251)    /// assert_eq!(result, "deep_fried");
[1252](https://docs.rs#1252)    /// ```
[1253](https://docs.rs#1253)    ///
[1254](https://docs.rs#1254)    /// Without the curly braces, the capture group name `first_` would be
[1255](https://docs.rs#1255)    /// used, and since it doesn't exist, it would be replaced with the empty
[1256](https://docs.rs#1256)    /// string.
[1257](https://docs.rs#1257)    ///
[1258](https://docs.rs#1258)    /// Finally, sometimes you just want to replace a literal string with no
[1259](https://docs.rs#1259)    /// regard for capturing group expansion. This can be done by wrapping a
[1260](https://docs.rs#1260)    /// byte string with `NoExpand`:
[1261](https://docs.rs#1261)    ///
[1262](https://docs.rs#1262)    /// ```rust
[1263](https://docs.rs#1263)    /// # use fancy_regex::Regex;
[1264](https://docs.rs#1264)    /// use fancy_regex::NoExpand;
[1265](https://docs.rs#1265)    ///
[1266](https://docs.rs#1266)    /// let re = Regex::new(r"(?P<last>[^,\s]+),\s+(\S+)").unwrap();
[1267](https://docs.rs#1267)    /// let result = re.replace("Springsteen, Bruce", NoExpand("$2 $last"));
[1268](https://docs.rs#1268)    /// assert_eq!(result, "$2 $last");
[1269](https://docs.rs#1269)    /// ```
[1270](https://docs.rs#1270)    pub fn replace<'t, R: Replacer>(&self, text: &'t str, rep: R) -> Cow<'t, str> {
[1271](https://docs.rs#1271)        self.replacen(text, 1, rep)
[1272](https://docs.rs#1272)    }
[1273](https://docs.rs#1273)
[1274](https://docs.rs#1274)    /// Replaces all non-overlapping matches in `text` with the replacement
[1275](https://docs.rs#1275)    /// provided. This is the same as calling `replacen` with `limit` set to
[1276](https://docs.rs#1276)    /// `0`.
[1277](https://docs.rs#1277)    ///
[1278](https://docs.rs#1278)    /// See the documentation for `replace` for details on how to access
[1279](https://docs.rs#1279)    /// capturing group matches in the replacement string.
[1280](https://docs.rs#1280)    pub fn replace_all<'t, R: Replacer>(&self, text: &'t str, rep: R) -> Cow<'t, str> {
[1281](https://docs.rs#1281)        self.replacen(text, 0, rep)
[1282](https://docs.rs#1282)    }
[1283](https://docs.rs#1283)
[1284](https://docs.rs#1284)    /// Replaces at most `limit` non-overlapping matches in `text` with the
[1285](https://docs.rs#1285)    /// replacement provided. If `limit` is 0, then all non-overlapping matches
[1286](https://docs.rs#1286)    /// are replaced.
[1287](https://docs.rs#1287)    ///
[1288](https://docs.rs#1288)    /// Will panic if any errors are encountered. Use `try_replacen`, which this
[1289](https://docs.rs#1289)    /// function unwraps, if you want to handle errors.
[1290](https://docs.rs#1290)    ///
[1291](https://docs.rs#1291)    /// See the documentation for `replace` for details on how to access
[1292](https://docs.rs#1292)    /// capturing group matches in the replacement string.
[1293](https://docs.rs#1293)    ///
[1294](https://docs.rs#1294)    pub fn replacen<'t, R: Replacer>(&self, text: &'t str, limit: usize, rep: R) -> Cow<'t, str> {
[1295](https://docs.rs#1295)        self.try_replacen(text, limit, rep).unwrap()
[1296](https://docs.rs#1296)    }
[1297](https://docs.rs#1297)
[1298](https://docs.rs#1298)    /// Replaces at most `limit` non-overlapping matches in `text` with the
[1299](https://docs.rs#1299)    /// replacement provided. If `limit` is 0, then all non-overlapping matches
[1300](https://docs.rs#1300)    /// are replaced.
[1301](https://docs.rs#1301)    ///
[1302](https://docs.rs#1302)    /// Propagates any errors encountered, such as `RuntimeError::BacktrackLimitExceeded`.
[1303](https://docs.rs#1303)    ///
[1304](https://docs.rs#1304)    /// See the documentation for `replace` for details on how to access
[1305](https://docs.rs#1305)    /// capturing group matches in the replacement string.
[1306](https://docs.rs#1306)    pub fn try_replacen<'t, R: Replacer>(
[1307](https://docs.rs#1307)        &self,
[1308](https://docs.rs#1308)        text: &'t str,
[1309](https://docs.rs#1309)        limit: usize,
[1310](https://docs.rs#1310)        mut rep: R,
[1311](https://docs.rs#1311)    ) -> Result<Cow<'t, str>> {
[1312](https://docs.rs#1312)        // If we know that the replacement doesn't have any capture expansions,
[1313](https://docs.rs#1313)        // then we can fast path. The fast path can make a tremendous
[1314](https://docs.rs#1314)        // difference:
[1315](https://docs.rs#1315)        //
[1316](https://docs.rs#1316)        //   1) We use `find_iter` instead of `captures_iter`. Not asking for
[1317](https://docs.rs#1317)        //      captures generally makes the regex engines faster.
[1318](https://docs.rs#1318)        //   2) We don't need to look up all of the capture groups and do
[1319](https://docs.rs#1319)        //      replacements inside the replacement string. We just push it
[1320](https://docs.rs#1320)        //      at each match and be done with it.
[1321](https://docs.rs#1321)        if let Some(rep) = rep.no_expansion() {
[1322](https://docs.rs#1322)            let mut it = self.find_iter(text).enumerate().peekable();
[1323](https://docs.rs#1323)            if it.peek().is_none() {
[1324](https://docs.rs#1324)                return Ok(Cow::Borrowed(text));
[1325](https://docs.rs#1325)            }
[1326](https://docs.rs#1326)            let mut new = String::with_capacity(text.len());
[1327](https://docs.rs#1327)            let mut last_match = 0;
[1328](https://docs.rs#1328)            for (i, m) in it {
[1329](https://docs.rs#1329)                let m = m?;
[1330](https://docs.rs#1330)
[1331](https://docs.rs#1331)                if limit > 0 && i >= limit {
[1332](https://docs.rs#1332)                    break;
[1333](https://docs.rs#1333)                }
[1334](https://docs.rs#1334)                new.push_str(&text[last_match..m.start()]);
[1335](https://docs.rs#1335)                new.push_str(&rep);
[1336](https://docs.rs#1336)                last_match = m.end();
[1337](https://docs.rs#1337)            }
[1338](https://docs.rs#1338)            new.push_str(&text[last_match..]);
[1339](https://docs.rs#1339)            return Ok(Cow::Owned(new));
[1340](https://docs.rs#1340)        }
[1341](https://docs.rs#1341)
[1342](https://docs.rs#1342)        // The slower path, which we use if the replacement needs access to
[1343](https://docs.rs#1343)        // capture groups.
[1344](https://docs.rs#1344)        let mut it = self.captures_iter(text).enumerate().peekable();
[1345](https://docs.rs#1345)        if it.peek().is_none() {
[1346](https://docs.rs#1346)            return Ok(Cow::Borrowed(text));
[1347](https://docs.rs#1347)        }
[1348](https://docs.rs#1348)        let mut new = String::with_capacity(text.len());
[1349](https://docs.rs#1349)        let mut last_match = 0;
[1350](https://docs.rs#1350)        for (i, cap) in it {
[1351](https://docs.rs#1351)            let cap = cap?;
[1352](https://docs.rs#1352)
[1353](https://docs.rs#1353)            if limit > 0 && i >= limit {
[1354](https://docs.rs#1354)                break;
[1355](https://docs.rs#1355)            }
[1356](https://docs.rs#1356)            // unwrap on 0 is OK because captures only reports matches
[1357](https://docs.rs#1357)            let m = cap.get(0).unwrap();
[1358](https://docs.rs#1358)            new.push_str(&text[last_match..m.start()]);
[1359](https://docs.rs#1359)            rep.replace_append(&cap, &mut new);
[1360](https://docs.rs#1360)            last_match = m.end();
[1361](https://docs.rs#1361)        }
[1362](https://docs.rs#1362)        new.push_str(&text[last_match..]);
[1363](https://docs.rs#1363)        Ok(Cow::Owned(new))
[1364](https://docs.rs#1364)    }
[1365](https://docs.rs#1365)
[1366](https://docs.rs#1366)    /// Splits the string by matches of the regex.
[1367](https://docs.rs#1367)    ///
[1368](https://docs.rs#1368)    /// Returns an iterator over the substrings of the target string
[1369](https://docs.rs#1369)    ///  that *aren't* matched by the regex.
[1370](https://docs.rs#1370)    ///

[1386](https://docs.rs#1386)            target,
[1387](https://docs.rs#1387)        }
[1388](https://docs.rs#1388)    }

[1478](https://docs.rs#1478)#[allow(clippy::len_without_is_empty)] // follow regex's API
[1479](https://docs.rs#1479)impl<'t> Captures<'t> {
[1480](https://docs.rs#1480)    /// Get the capture group by its index in the regex.
[1481](https://docs.rs#1481)    ///
[1482](https://docs.rs#1482)    /// If there is no match for that group or the index does not correspond to a group, `None` is
[1483](https://docs.rs#1483)    /// returned. The index 0 returns the whole match.
[1484](https://docs.rs#1484)    pub fn get(&self, i: usize) -> Option<Match<'t>> {
[1485](https://docs.rs#1485)        match &self.inner {
[1486](https://docs.rs#1486)            CapturesImpl::Wrap {
[1487](https://docs.rs#1487)                text,
[1488](https://docs.rs#1488)                locations,
[1489](https://docs.rs#1489)                explicit_capture_group_0,
[1490](https://docs.rs#1490)            } => locations
[1491](https://docs.rs#1491)                .get_group(i + if *explicit_capture_group_0 { 1 } else { 0 })
[1492](https://docs.rs#1492)                .map(|span| Match {
[1493](https://docs.rs#1493)                    text,
[1494](https://docs.rs#1494)                    start: span.start,
[1495](https://docs.rs#1495)                    end: span.end,
[1496](https://docs.rs#1496)                }),
[1497](https://docs.rs#1497)            CapturesImpl::Fancy { text, saves } => {
[1498](https://docs.rs#1498)                let slot = i * 2;
[1499](https://docs.rs#1499)                if slot >= saves.len() {
[1500](https://docs.rs#1500)                    return None;
[1501](https://docs.rs#1501)                }
[1502](https://docs.rs#1502)                let lo = saves[slot];
[1503](https://docs.rs#1503)                if lo == usize::MAX {
[1504](https://docs.rs#1504)                    return None;
[1505](https://docs.rs#1505)                }
[1506](https://docs.rs#1506)                let hi = saves[slot + 1];
[1507](https://docs.rs#1507)                Some(Match {
[1508](https://docs.rs#1508)                    text,
[1509](https://docs.rs#1509)                    start: lo,
[1510](https://docs.rs#1510)                    end: hi,
[1511](https://docs.rs#1511)                })
[1512](https://docs.rs#1512)            }
[1513](https://docs.rs#1513)        }
[1514](https://docs.rs#1514)    }
[1515](https://docs.rs#1515)
[1516](https://docs.rs#1516)    /// Returns the match for a named capture group.  Returns `None` the capture
[1517](https://docs.rs#1517)    /// group did not match or if there is no group with the given name.
[1518](https://docs.rs#1518)    pub fn name(&self, name: &str) -> Option<Match<'t>> {
[1519](https://docs.rs#1519)        self.named_groups.get(name).and_then(|i| self.get(*i))
[1520](https://docs.rs#1520)    }
[1521](https://docs.rs#1521)
[1522](https://docs.rs#1522)    /// Expands all instances of `$group` in `replacement` to the corresponding
[1523](https://docs.rs#1523)    /// capture group `name`, and writes them to the `dst` buffer given.
[1524](https://docs.rs#1524)    ///
[1525](https://docs.rs#1525)    /// `group` may be an integer corresponding to the index of the
[1526](https://docs.rs#1526)    /// capture group (counted by order of opening parenthesis where `\0` is the
[1527](https://docs.rs#1527)    /// entire match) or it can be a name (consisting of letters, digits or
[1528](https://docs.rs#1528)    /// underscores) corresponding to a named capture group.
[1529](https://docs.rs#1529)    ///
[1530](https://docs.rs#1530)    /// If `group` isn't a valid capture group (whether the name doesn't exist
[1531](https://docs.rs#1531)    /// or isn't a valid index), then it is replaced with the empty string.
[1532](https://docs.rs#1532)    ///
[1533](https://docs.rs#1533)    /// The longest possible name is used. e.g., `$1a` looks up the capture
[1534](https://docs.rs#1534)    /// group named `1a` and not the capture group at index `1`. To exert more
[1535](https://docs.rs#1535)    /// precise control over the name, use braces, e.g., `${1}a`.
[1536](https://docs.rs#1536)    ///
[1537](https://docs.rs#1537)    /// To write a literal `$`, use `$$`.
[1538](https://docs.rs#1538)    ///
[1539](https://docs.rs#1539)    /// For more control over expansion, see [`Expander`].
[1540](https://docs.rs#1540)    ///
[1541](https://docs.rs#1541)    /// [`Expander`]: expand/struct.Expander.html
[1542](https://docs.rs#1542)    pub fn expand(&self, replacement: &str, dst: &mut String) {
[1543](https://docs.rs#1543)        Expander::default().append_expansion(dst, replacement, self);
[1544](https://docs.rs#1544)    }
[1545](https://docs.rs#1545)
[1546](https://docs.rs#1546)    /// Iterate over the captured groups in order in which they appeared in the regex. The first
[1547](https://docs.rs#1547)    /// capture corresponds to the whole match.
[1548](https://docs.rs#1548)    pub fn iter<'c>(&'c self) -> SubCaptureMatches<'c, 't> {
[1549](https://docs.rs#1549)        SubCaptureMatches { caps: self, i: 0 }
[1550](https://docs.rs#1550)    }
[1551](https://docs.rs#1551)
[1552](https://docs.rs#1552)    /// How many groups were captured. This is always at least 1 because group 0 returns the whole
[1553](https://docs.rs#1553)    /// match.
[1554](https://docs.rs#1554)    pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
[1555](https://docs.rs#1555)        match &self.inner {
[1556](https://docs.rs#1556)            CapturesImpl::Wrap {
[1557](https://docs.rs#1557)                locations,
[1558](https://docs.rs#1558)                explicit_capture_group_0,
[1559](https://docs.rs#1559)                ..
[1560](https://docs.rs#1560)            } => locations.group_len() - if *explicit_capture_group_0 { 1 } else { 0 },
[1561](https://docs.rs#1561)            CapturesImpl::Fancy { saves, .. } => saves.len() / 2,
[1562](https://docs.rs#1562)        }
[1563](https://docs.rs#1563)    }
[1564](https://docs.rs#1564)}
[1565](https://docs.rs#1565)
[1566](https://docs.rs#1566)/// Get a group by index.

[1577](https://docs.rs#1577)impl<'t> Index<usize> for Captures<'t> {

[1609](https://docs.rs#1609)impl<'c, 't> Iterator for SubCaptureMatches<'c, 't> {
[1610](https://docs.rs#1610)    type Item = Option<Match<'t>>;
[1611](https://docs.rs#1611)
[1612](https://docs.rs#1612)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Option<Match<'t>>> {
[1613](https://docs.rs#1613)        if self.i < self.caps.len() {
[1614](https://docs.rs#1614)            let result = self.caps.get(self.i);
[1615](https://docs.rs#1615)            self.i += 1;
[1616](https://docs.rs#1616)            Some(result)

[1619](https://docs.rs#1619)        }
[1620](https://docs.rs#1620)    }
